So I went out to a trout lake today, it's the first day of whats looking to be at least a week long heatwave, it was about 86F today 30C, now I knew this was going to happen but I was hoping to get a couple days in first. What happened was lake turnover, basically what that means is the lakes a mess, everythings everywhere, algae, moss, bugs, baitfish, it;s like somebody took a giant spoon and stirred the lake up. If you ever see it happen unless you like burning hours for no reason like I do you might as well go home.

imagine a lake as a huge glass of water, some cooking oil, maybe some gasoline, some diesel and some motor oil(sounds gross but they are different densities and will form visible layers when settled), a lake is made the same way but of water with varying temperatures and what separates them normally is a line called the thermocline, it's the line where warmer surface temperatures of summer and the colder deep temperatures meet and buffer. there are other layers but the thermocline is the active layer. but if yoy kix all the fluids I named in the glass and let it settle you'd see visible layers of each fluid, the lake is the same way but when it gets hot the top layer heats up and heats up and presses on the thermocline and eventually it bursts and stirs EVERYTHING the fuck up. causes currents(all water temperatures just want to stablize) and all kinds of fucked up shit to happen, loosens loose moss and algae, stirs up bugs and baitfish, it's like taking that layered glass and stirring it, everythings everywhere and it's a mess, the food is everywhere the fish are everywhere and the visibility is garbage.

This probably effects all types of fish in all types of lakes but in a trout lake it's everything. Trout associate with temperature and oxygen, not with surface or bottom, so when the lake stirs up the trout stir up, yesterday the lakes were fine, I went out but didn't take pictures and caught 2 nice splake 19 and 20 inches and about 10 brookies that were too small for me to keep from the stocked ponds(13 inches)

Anyways it looks like it's more creeking and maybe walleye/pike fishing until the ponds settle again. Creeking during a heatwave sounds like hard work, but it's my true passion so we'll see.

When I was about 12 or so, my family was out fishing on Lake of the Woods. It was an over cast day, so not very warm at all (20C maybe). My younger brother accidentally let go of his rod when casting and to the bottom of the lake it went. A couple of minutes later the sun poked through the clouds and we could see the bottom, and the rod. My dad told me to go get it, and that it was only 15 feet deep. (No fish finders back in those days). It was much deeper, 30-40 feet. I dove down and somewhere around 20 feet, I passed the first thermocline. God damn was that a shock of cold water, like right to the bones. I did not want to fail and be told to go back down and do this again, so I fought through, grabbed a piece of the rod, planted my feet on the ground (which was some slimy plants) and jumped as hard as I could and shot back up to the surface, broke the water and got my body halfway into the boat. I was only under the water for less than 30 seconds (at that age, I used to practice holding my breath and compete with people, I could hold it for 100 seconds, swim underwater the length of pools etc), but was gasping for air, and freezing, which prompted my dad to tell me to stop being such a wimp.

Long story short, those temperature changes in lakes are very pronounced and the water is much colder than you imagine, even if you can see the bottom.
